title: Historia Ecclesiastica Vocata Tripartita
author: Cassiodorus
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1180.tmp1180.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Compensas autem recitantibus et tuo judicio, et favoribus opportunis, nec non aureis imaginibus, et positione simulacrorum, et donis, et honoribus universis. Qualem vero te circa recitantes præbes, tales dudum fuerunt judices [ed., Niv., judices Cretes] circa dulciloquum Homerum: aut Alevadse [alii, Alevasj circa Simonidem; aut Dionysius Siciliæ tyrannus circa Platonem Socratis discipulum ; aut Philippus Macedo circa Theopompum historiographum; aut Severus Cæsar circa Oppianum, qui metris genera piscium et naturas, captionemque na- ravit.
passages.english: And you reward those who give readings both with your judgement and with timely applause, and also with golden images, the setting up of statues, gifts, and every kind of honour. Such as you show yourself toward those who give readings, such long ago were the judges [of Crete] toward sweet-voiced Homer; or the Aleuadae toward Simonides; or Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, toward Plato the disciple of Socrates; or Philip of Macedon toward Theopompus the historian; or the Caesar Severus toward Oppian, who told in verse the kinds and natures of fishes and the catching of them.
passages.notes: Editorial variants in the text: "judices Cretes" (one edition) and "Alevas" (others) for "Alevadae"; the Aleuadae are the Thessalian noble family, patrons of Simonides. "Severus Caesar": Oppian's patron is traditionally an emperor of the Severan house. "na- ravit" read as "narravit".

passages.original: Cousona his direxit et Philogonio Antiochenae præsuli civitatis, et Eustathio, qui tunc Berœnsem gubernabat Ecclesiam, et ainis apostolicorum dogmatum defensoribus. Sed neque Arius quiescere passus est; scripsit enim et ipse concordibus suis. Quia vero nihil falsi contra eum scripsit sacratissimus Alexander, ipse Arius litteris suis scriptis ad Nicomediensem Eusebium protestatus est. Quam epistolam inserere non omittam, ut communicatores impietatis ejus ignorantibus possim facere manifestos. THEODORETUS, lib. I, c.
passages.english: He sent letters to the same effect to Philogonius, bishop of the city of Antioch, and to Eustathius, who was then governing the Church of Beroea, and to the other defenders of the apostolic doctrines. But Arius did not allow himself to rest either; for he too wrote to those who agreed with him. And that the most holy Alexander wrote nothing false against him, Arius himself testified in the letter he wrote to Eusebius of Nicomedia. I will not fail to insert this letter, so that I may make plain to those who do not know them who the sharers in his impiety were. Theodoret, book I, chapter
passages.notes: "Cousona" is read as "Consona" (letters in agreement, to the same effect), and "ainis" as "aliis" (others); both are scanning errors. The final source reference continues in the following context ("4, p. 8").

passages.original: Hujus autem concertator, et veritatis propugnaculi turris Athanasius, successor Alexandri famosissimi præsulis, quando scripsit ad Afros, eliam haec adjecit : Convenientes enim episcopi studuerunt verba quidem impietatis ab Arianis inventa perimere. Ime est, ,ex non existenlihus, et quod dicebant, creaturam et facturam Filium;
passages.english: His fellow combatant, and the tower of the bulwark of truth, Athanasius, successor of Alexander the most renowned bishop, when he wrote to the Africans, also added this: "For the bishops, assembling, were eager to do away with the impious words invented by the Arians, that is, 'from things that do not exist', and their saying that the Son was a creature and a thing made;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "eliam" = etiam; "Ime est" = id est; "existenlihus" = existentibus.

passages.original: Quomodo Eusebius et Theogonius, dato pœnitentiæ libello, recepti sunt.
passages.english: How Eusebius and Theogonius were received back after submitting a statement of repentance.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: Quomodo sit Arius ab exsilio revocatus, et qualem libellum dederit Constantino , et de fraudibus Arianorum.
passages.english: How Arius was recalled from exile, and what kind of statement he gave to Constantine, and on the deceits of the Arians.
passages.notes: "Libellum" may mean a written statement or petition; here it probably refers to a statement of faith.

passages.original: Epistola Constantini evocantis episcopos, ut Athanasii causas ipse cognosceret.
passages.english: Letter of Constantine summoning the bishops, so that he might himself hear the case of Athanasius.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: Quomodo Athanasius favore Constantini minoris Alexandriam remeaverit, et ejusdem Constantin; epistola-
passages.english: How Athanasius returned to Alexandria through the favour of Constantine the younger, and the letter of the same Constantine.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: Quomodo Athanasius, Arianis bella sibi denuo suscitanlibus, ad partes discesserit Italiæ.
passages.english: How Athanasius, when the Arians again stirred up wars against him, departed to the regions of Italy.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: et non solum iEgyptum, sed etiam Pakestinam, et Phoenicen, vicinasque gentes ejus gratia dicebant esse turbatas. Proinde hujusmodi verbis levissimam obsidentes imperatoris intentionem, suaserunt ut Athanasium ab Ecclesia rursus expellere;. Qui agnoscens eorum consilium, ad partes Hesperias abiit. THEODORETUS, lib. n, cap. 3, p. 70.
passages.english: and they said that not only Egypt but also Palestine and Phoenicia and the neighbouring peoples were thrown into turmoil on his account. Accordingly, besieging the emperor's very fickle mind with words of this kind, they persuaded [him] to expel Athanasius from the Church again. He, recognising their plan, went away to the western regions. Theodoret, book 2, chapter 3, p. 70.
passages.notes: "expellere;" read as "expelleret".

passages.original: Non tamen ab Ariana peste Ecclesia Ii. berata est. Nam Leontius post eum ordinatur, genere Phrygius, voluntate nequissimus. Verum Constanlius ea quae contra episcopos fuerant machinata, eiperimento cognoscens, scripsit Athanasio maximo et semel, et secundo, et tertio , invitans eum ut a 254 partibus remearet Hesperiis, sicut ipsis litteris indicatur. THEODORETUS, lib. II, cap. 8, 9 et 10, p. 83,84.
passages.english: Yet the Church was not freed from the Arian plague. For after him Leontius was ordained, a Phrygian by birth, most wicked in disposition. But Constantius, learning by experience what had been contrived against the bishops, wrote to the great Athanasius once, a second time, and a third, inviting him to return from the western regions, as is shown by the letters themselves. Theodoret, book 2, chapters 8, 9 and 10, pp. 83, 84.
passages.notes: "254" is a stray page number from the printed edition, omitted.

passages.original: Epistola Constantii ad Alexandrinos, ut reciperent Athanasium.
passages.english: Letter of Constantius to the Alexandrians, that they should receive Athanasius.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: Quomodo Athanasius Alexandriam sit reversus.
passages.english: How Athanasius returned to Alexandria.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: Super hæc igilur Athanasius etiam consolatorios libros virginibus illis scripsit quæ crudelissimas pertulerunt passiones, dicens inter hæc : Propterea nemo vestrum sit tristis, licet et sepulturam vobis denegent impii et prohibeant vos eflerri. Nani usque ad hoc nequitia pervenit Arianorum, ut et portas clauderent, et circa sepulturarum loca, veluti dæmones, residerent, nc quis sepeliretur fidelium dilectorum [mi.
passages.english: In addition to this, therefore, Athanasius also wrote books of consolation to those virgins who had endured the most cruel sufferings, saying among other things: "Therefore let none of you be sad, even though the impious deny you burial and forbid you to be carried out [for burial]. For the wickedness of the Arians has reached such a point that they even closed the gates and sat around the burial places like demons, so that none of the beloved faithful might be buried."
passages.notes: The text ends with an editorial apparatus note, '[mi. Lyr., electorum]' (continued in the following context), recording a variant 'electorum' ('of the elect faithful') for 'dilectorum'; this note is not translated. 'eflerri' read as 'efferri', 'Nani' as 'Nam'.

passages.original: Quomodo Athanasius furorem Constantii denuo decli- naverit.
passages.english: How Athanasius again escaped the fury of Constantius.
passages.notes: Chapter heading.

passages.original: Sed Pt maximus Athanasius in epistola quam scripsit ad Afros, taliter de Ariminensi concilio disputavit.
passages.english: But the most great Athanasius, in the letter he wrote to the Africans, discussed the Council of Ariminum as follows.
passages.notes: 'Pt' is probably a scanning error for 'et' or a stray mark; it is left untranslated.

passages.original: Quid sophista Libanius contra Christianos scripserit, et quomodo Socrates.historiographus ejus dicta con- futarit.
passages.english: What the sophist Libanius wrote against the Christians, and how Socrates the historian refuted his statements.

passages.original: V.et Frob., Jovinianus] ergo imperator, mox ut imperii sui terras ingressus est, primum haec conscripsit, ut episcopi de exsilio remearent, et Ec- ctesias eis reddendas esse professus est qui exposl- tam in Nicaea fidem inviolabiliter servaverunt. Scripsit etiam Athanasio, qui præcipuus erat horum doa- matum propugnator : petens ut ei rescriberet perfectam divinorum dogmatum disciplinam. Qui elo- quentiores episeopos congregans rescripsit : rogans ut fidem Nicææ expositam eustodiret , tanquam apostolicis degmatibus congruentem.
passages.english: So the emperor, as soon as he entered the lands of his empire, first wrote these instructions: that the bishops should return from exile. He also declared that churches were to be restored to those who had kept inviolate the faith set out at Nicaea. He also wrote to Athanasius, who was the foremost champion of these doctrines, asking him to write back a complete teaching of the divine doctrines. Athanasius gathered the more eloquent bishops and wrote back, asking him to keep the faith set out at Nicaea, as being in accord with the apostolic doctrines.
passages.notes: The passage opens mid-way through an editorial note: the edition reads 'Jovianus', and the note records 'Jovinianus' as the reading of the Venice and Froben editions. The emperor is Jovian.

passages.original: Et humt- nam quidem etiam passibiles suscipere poterunt, divinæ impassibiles tantummodo sum capaces, qui etiam orationis tempore proprio mentis lumine resplen- cientes semetipso; inspiciunt. Ægyptiorumvcro sacratissima lux Athanasius ait: Præcepit Moyses mensam contra aquilonis constitui partem. Quamob. rem cognoscant contemplativi quis est qui contra eos spiret, et omnem tentationem forti mente susti- neant, et cum alacritate ad se accedentes enutriant, .
passages.english: And human [knowledge] they will be able to receive even while they are subject to passions, but they are capable of divine [knowledge] only when free from passion; they, even at the time of prayer, shining with the mind's own light, behold themselves. And Athanasius, the most sacred light of the Egyptians, says: "Moses commanded that the table be set toward the northern side. Therefore let the contemplatives recognize who it is that blows against them, and let them endure every temptation with a strong mind, and with eagerness nourish those who come to them."
passages.notes: The first sentence is elliptical; 'scientias' (knowledge) is supplied from the preceding context. 'semetipso; inspiciunt' read as 'semetipsos inspiciunt'. 'sum capaces' read as 'sunt capaces'.

passages.original: Ego autem lamentor et ge- mo calamitatem meam : quia servis quidem et rnen- dicantibus aperta sunt templa Dei , et proprium Dominum ingredientes ticenter exorant, mihi vero ingressus ad eum non est. insuper etiam caeli sunt mihi clausi. Hæc dicens, verba singula singultibus interrumpebat. Tunc Rufinus : Curro, inquit, si Libi placet, pontificique precibus persuadeo ut solvatur liuculum quod ligavit. Ait imperator : Non suadebis Ambrosio. Novi ego decretum illius esse justum, neque reverebitur imperialem potentiam, ut legem possit prævaricari divinam.
passages.english: "But I lament and groan over my misfortune: for to slaves and beggars the temples of God are open, and entering they freely entreat their own Lord, but for me there is no entry to him. Moreover, the heavens too are closed to me." Saying this, he broke up each word with sobs. Then Rufinus said: "I will run, if it pleases you, and persuade the bishop by entreaties to loose the bond that he has bound." The emperor said: "You will not persuade Ambrose. I know that his decree is just, and he will not so respect imperial power as to be able to transgress the divine law."
passages.notes: 'ticenter' read as 'licenter'; 'Libi' as 'tibi'; 'liuculum' as 'vinculum'.

passages.original: Tunc antistes: Quam, Inquit, pœnitentiam ostendisti post tantas iniquitates! Quibus medicaminibus incurabilia vulnera plagasque cu. rasti ? At imperator: Tuum, inquit, opus est et do. cere, et medicamina temperare ; meum vero oblata suscipere.. Tunc sanctus Ambrosius: Quoniam furori, inquit, tuum judicium commisisti, et non ratio protulit sententiam, sed potius iracundia: scribe le- Bem quae decreta furoris evacuet., ut triginta diebus sententia necis atque proscriptionis in litteris tantummodo maneat, et judicium rationis exspectet;
passages.english: Then the bishop said: "What penance have you shown after such great iniquities? With what remedies have you healed incurable wounds and blows?" And the emperor said: "It is your task both to teach and to mix the remedies; mine to accept what is offered." Then Saint Ambrose said: "Since you entrusted your judgement to fury, and it was not reason that pronounced the sentence but rather anger, write a law that will make void the decrees of fury, so that for thirty days a sentence of death and of proscription will remain only in writing and will await the judgement of reason;

passages.original: Timotheum itaque ego ipse vidi, et cognovi quemadmodum interrogantibus crat respondere paratus: solvens obscurissimas quaestiones quæ in divinis inveniuntur eloquiis, testem vocans veracissi- mum Orig -nem. Mihi tamen videtur admirabile me quomodo tales viri in Arianorum lege manserunt, 'tuorum unus quidem Platonem semper h ibebat in manibus, aller respiciebat jugiter Origenem : dum nusquam Plato secundam vel tertiam causam, sicut ipse nominare solet, inituin subsistentiæ asserat percepisse; et Origeues coæternum ubique fateatur Iilium Patri. Qui licet in sua sententia manserint, religionem tamen Arianam perduxerunt latenter ad meliora.
passages.english: I myself saw Timothy, and learned how ready he was to answer those who questioned him, solving the most obscure questions found in the divine scriptures, and calling Origen as a most truthful witness. Yet it seems remarkable to me how such men remained in the Arian creed, one of whom always had Plato in his hands, the other constantly looked to Origen; since Plato nowhere asserts that the second or third cause, as he himself is accustomed to call it, received a beginning of existence, and Origen everywhere acknowledges the Son to be coeternal with the Father. Although they remained in their own opinion, they nevertheless quietly led the Arian religion towards better things.
passages.notes: 'admirabile me' likely a scanning error ('mihi... admirabile') ; 'me' omitted.

passages.original: Nam dum quidam portus in ore Ponti Euxini constitutus, ex antiquo Pharmacus appellaretur, id cst venenarius, mulato nomine eum locum Sanatorium nominavit : lie dum ibi collectae praedicarentur, nomine blasphemo lucus ipse designaretur. Sed et alium locum Argyropolim pro bujusmodi causa nominavit. Chrysopolis enim in capite Bosphori constituta est, cujus multi antiquorum faciunt mentionem. De qua civitate Xenophon in primo libro Helladicorum dicit, quia eain mutavit Alcibiades, et in ea constituit ut qui navigabant de Ponto, decimas ibi praeberent. Videns ergo Att cus locum in contraria ripa Chrysopoleos positum, delectabilem et decorum, ait : Argyropolis nominetur;
passages.english: For since a certain harbour situated at the mouth of the Euxine Sea had from of old been called Pharmacus, that is, 'the Poisoner', he changed the name and called that place 'the Healing Place', so that, when assemblies were announced there, the place itself would not be designated by a blasphemous name. He also named another place Argyropolis for a similar reason. For Chrysopolis is situated at the head of the Bosporus, and many of the ancients mention it. About this city Xenophon says in the first book of the Hellenica that Alcibiades changed it and established in it that those sailing from the Pontus should pay tithes there. So Atticus, seeing that the place situated on the opposite bank from Chrysopolis was delightful and beautiful, said: "Let it be named Argyropolis";
passages.notes: 'Sanatorium' renders Greek Therapeia ('healing'). 'lucus' read as 'locus'. 'mutavit' (changed) probably renders a Greek word for 'fortified' (Xenophon says Alcibiades walled it); the Latin as given says 'changed'. Argyropolis = 'Silver City', contrasted with Chrysopolis, 'Gold City'.
